content.text: Research Overview: Human vs. AI Creativity in Game Design
Format: Academic Paper (IEEE Standards)
Core Inquiry: A comparative analysis of creative outputs between human designers and generative AI models within the context of game mechanics and world-building.
Key Objective: Determining the current boundaries of AI as a co-creative tool and identifying the unique "human-centric" design elements that remain difficult for algorithmic models to replicate.
Abstract & Thesis

The research explores the intersection of procedural generation and human intuition. It investigates whether AI can transcend "recombinational creativity" (mixing existing data) to achieve "transformational creativity" (creating entirely new design paradigms) in game development. The paper analyzes specific design tasks—ranging from level layout to narrative branching—to evaluate the qualitative differences in the resulting player experience.
Comparative Methodology
The study employs a structured framework to compare design outputs based on three primary pillars:
Structural Coherence: How well the design follows the functional constraints of game logic and player progression.
Thematic Resonance: The ability of the design to evoke specific emotional responses and maintain narrative consistency.
Innovation vs. Imitation: Assessing if the AI-generated content offers novel mechanics or merely mimics high-frequency patterns found in its training data.
Key Findings & Insights

The "Intentionality" Gap: While AI excels at rapid iteration and generating vast amounts of coherent content, it lacks "intentionality"—the ability to break rules for a specific emotional or artistic purpose.

Co-Creativity Model: The research concludes that the most effective use of AI in modern game design is not as a replacement for the designer, but as a "force multiplier" that handles procedural density, allowing the human designer to focus on high-level systems and emotional anchoring.
Iterative Design: Highlighting how AI can be utilized to stress-test game balance through rapid prototyping, significantly reducing the pre-production phase of complex system design.

Project Overview: Dissonance Ward (Working Title)
Genre: Procedural Horror / Puzzle
The Core Concept: A system-driven horror experience set in a hospital, combining the tension of anomaly detection with a roguelike map structure.
My Role: Concept & System Designer

Design Highlights: The game utilizes a 5x5 procedural grid map, ensuring no two playthroughs are the same. To survive, players must navigate through shifting environments, identify subtle anomalies, and manage a unique "multiple character personalities" mechanic that directly affects how the world is perceived and interacted with.
The Roguelike Grid: 5x5 Procedural Map
Instead of a linear hallway, the game utilizes a modular spatial puzzle.
Dynamic Navigation: The hospital is generated as a 5x5 grid of rooms. Moving between rooms requires making directional choices based on environmental clues.

The Loop: Failing to identify an anomaly or making the wrong directional choice shifts the grid. This resets progress or teleports the player to a more hostile section of the map, adding strong roguelike tension to the exploration.
Observation-Based Horror & Anomalies
Combat is non-existent; the player's only weapon is their memory and attention to detail.
Subtle Shifts: Rooms establish a "baseline" state. The player must spot deviations—ranging from displaced medical equipment and shifting shadows to architectural impossibilities.
Risk vs. Reward: Correctly identifying an anomaly grants safe passage closer to the exit, while failing to notice them triggers psychological deterioration or enemy encounters.
The Multi-Personality Mechanic (Perception Shift)
The standout systemic feature of the game is the protagonist's fractured psychological state.
Mechanic Impact: The active personality fundamentally changes how the game world is perceived. An anomaly that is invisible to one personality might be glaringly obvious to another.

Strategic Balancing: Forcing a personality switch is not free; it might trigger specific phobias, audio-visual hallucinations, or movement constraints. The player must constantly balance their psychological state against the environmental puzzles.

bartle-poe.title: Bartle’s Player Taxonomy: A Path of Exile Case Study

content.text: Video Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YNn5dXeQU1Q
Bartle’s taxonomy of player types provides a highly effective framework for analyzing player engagement, particularly in a complex game like Path of Exile.

Explorer type players, who prioritize discovering a game's world, lore, mechanics, and systems, find immense depth in this title. The game features a massive passive skill tree and a system where various skills are socketed directly into equipment. Since these skills are remarkably abundant, the system presents players with countless unique combinations to experiment with. Furthermore, beyond its intricate mechanics, Path of Exile offers a satisfying narrative progression, diverse environments, and compelling bosses, making it a highly attractive experience for Explorers.

Achievers focus primarily on accomplishments and challenges within the game. In Path of Exile, dedicated tabs explicitly display the milestones players can earn. There are 123 achievements available across any league, alongside objectives specific to individual leagues. While these league challenges generally appear more difficult to accomplish, a significant portion of both categories essentially require players to perform routine gameplay activities in a slightly more specific manner. Milestones such as reaching a certain level or defeating a particular boss with a designated class are quite common. Additionally, there are notorious achievements within the community, such as No Stones Unturned, which requires players to click on every single lore text object scattered across the maps. For players who do not inherently lean towards the Achiever profile, these types of milestones may not seem particularly exciting when there is already an overwhelming amount of content left to discover.

Socializer types consist of players who prefer playing with friends, seeking social interaction just as much as the gameplay itself, and enjoying discussions about the titles they play. Since it is entirely possible to play the campaign cooperatively from start to finish, the game serves as an enjoyable option for this demographic. Furthermore, Path of Exile boasts a massive player base and an internal economic system that closely mirrors real life economics. Items known as Chaos Orbs are utilized essentially as a primary currency for trading, and this trading economy becomes crucial for progressing and acquiring desired gear. Therefore, Socializers have ample opportunities not only for cooperative play but also for communicating, interacting, and discussing the market with the broader community.

Finally, Killer players are generally those who thrive on competition and take pleasure in dominating or sabotaging their peers. Path of Exile does offer a PVP mode that might attract this type of player, but since the title does not possess a traditional MMORPG structure, combat between players is strictly confined to designated PVP arenas. Consequently, there is no opportunity to attack others while progressing through the main world. However, if a player's mindset is focused on destroying absolutely everything in sight rather than strictly targeting other players, Path of Exile acts as a quintessential ARPG. Eradicating the massive hordes of enemies the game constantly throws at players, especially in the later stages, can certainly satisfy that inherent desire for destruction.

Project Overview: Idle Economy & Progression Modeling
Genre: Idle / Incremental Game Economy
The Challenge: Designing and balancing a 15-minute (900 seconds) progression simulation with exponentially scaling upgrade costs.
My Role: Systems & Economy Designer
Tools Used: Excel (Data Modeling), Python (Algorithmic Testing), Unity (Playable APK and EXE Build)
Project Files: [Download Playable APK] | [View Excel Simulation Model] | [View Python Scripts]
Idle_Game.xlsx
The Design Problem: Exponential Scaling vs. Time

Idle games are built on a delicate balance between active/passive income and delayed gratification. In this project, I created a rigorous mathematical model to simulate exactly 15 minutes of gameplay.

The core mechanics rely on six tiers of upgrades (from Small Mines to Alchemical Mines), where the cost of each building scales exponentially based on ownership. The formula dictating this inflation is:
Cost = BaseCost*1.1^N
(Where N is the number of that specific mine type already owned).

The design challenge was to find the absolute "optimal path" to reach the maximum possible gold at turn 901. To solve this, I built a detailed spreadsheet tracking second-by-second income, cumulative costs, and purchasing decisions.
Man vs. Machine: Why Algorithms Fail at Idle Games

To find the perfect progression curve, I didn't rely solely on manual playtesting. I developed Python algorithms to calculate the highest possible yield and attempted to use Excel Solver. However, the results revealed a fascinating reality about game design: Human intuition consistently outperformed the algorithms.
Both my own manual playthroughs and the playtest data from other players yielded significantly higher final gold counts than the Python scripts. Here is the systemic breakdown of why this happens:

The "Local Optima" Trap: Most standard optimization algorithms (like Greedy algorithms) evaluate the immediate Return on Investment (ROI). If a Small Mine offers the best cost-to-income ratio at second 45, the algorithm buys it. However, it gets stuck in "local optima," constantly buying cheap upgrades and delaying massive power spikes.

Combinatorial Explosion: The sheer volume of possibilities across 900 seconds with 6 variable upgrade paths creates a mathematical web too vast for simple solvers (like Excel Solver) to compute brute-force.

The Power of Delayed Gratification: Human players naturally understand macro-strategy. A human can look at the board and decide, "I will buy absolutely nothing for the next 40 seconds to save up for a Huge Mine." Humans willingly accept a mathematically "sub-optimal" period of low income because they intuitively understand that the massive exponential spike later will eclipse short-term losses.
Design Takeaway

This experiment proved that a well-designed idle game cannot be balanced purely by running automated scripts. True progression design requires understanding the player's psychological willingness to "wait for the big reward." The APK provided here is the playable manifestation of this very economic model, allowing players to test their own delayed gratification against the math.

settlers-of-catan.title: An Analysis of Settlers of Catan

content.text: Video Link: https://youtu.be/oR9vTZPhRNk
Story

Narrative depth is not one of Catan’s primary focuses or strengths. The sole narrative context we can extract from the game is that we act as administrators or settlers, striving to gather resources by establishing villages and cities, with the ultimate goal of developing these settlements to a specific tier before rival leaders do.
Aesthetics

Although Catan has refreshed its visual design in recent editions, it remains an older title and still retains its classic atmosphere. However, the game leverages its design brilliantly to serve its mechanics and gameplay.
Functional Borders

Unlike many resource management games that also utilize modular hexagonal maps, such as Terraforming Mars, Catan encloses these tiles within a fixed border. This not only prevents the tiles from sliding but also integrates the outer frame into the map itself, giving it a functional purpose. Consequently, it stops the randomly arranged hexagons from shifting mid-game, preventing the roads, settlements, and cities placed on top from falling apart.
Minimalist UI

Furthermore, unlike its contemporaries, the perimeter of the game board lacks any victory point tracks or secondary indicators. As a player, I personally dislike such tracking boards and prefer to keep score mentally, so I highly appreciate this design choice.
Mechanics
Catan perfectly exemplifies the adage "easy to learn, hard to master." The core mechanics actively utilized by players are limited to rolling dice, trading, and building.
Resource Generation

On each turn, the active player rolls two dice; any player with a settlement or city adjacent to the hexagonal tile displaying the rolled sum gathers the corresponding resource. It is safe to say that rolling dice to accumulate resources is Catan’s most fundamental mechanic. Yet, this system is so ingeniously designed that it is precisely what makes the game simple to grasp but difficult to master. The completely randomized placement of both the terrain tiles and the number tokens dictates that entirely different tactical approaches must be formulated for every single session. Striving to build around areas with the highest statistical probability of resource generation, while simultaneously anticipating the robber, transforms Catan into a profoundly deep strategy game.
Construction

Beyond this, building is an indispensable mechanic. By spending specific combinations of resources, players can construct roads, settlements, and cities. While you are not obligated to use this mechanic every turn, it is mathematically impossible to win without building anything. Considering you start with two points, if you somehow manage to only buy development cards without constructing new structures, even acquiring the "Largest Army" card and all five standalone victory point cards would leave you stuck at 9 points, just shy of a victory.
Trading Dynamics

Trading, on the other hand, is arguably the primary reason Catan stands out as a highly social game. During your turn, you can attempt to acquire the resources you need by trading the ones you have with other players. While the rulebook explicitly states that resources cannot be gifted, there is no rule preventing players from making heavily skewed or "rip-off" trades. If no mutual agreement can be reached with the players, you can always trade with the bank at a 4:1 ratio. This ratio can be reduced to 3:1, or even 2:1 for a specific resource, if you have a settlement or city adjacent to the relevant harbor. Although trading tends to happen more frequently than building in any given turn, achieving victory without executing a single trade is not entirely impossible, provided you have a lucky terrain layout and optimally placed settlements.
The Robber

Moreover, there is the robber mechanic. While there is a statistically minute chance it might never appear throughout a game, we encounter it frequently since its trigger condition is rolling a 7. When activated, by moving the robber to a terrain hex of your choice, you not only block that hex from producing resources but also steal a resource card from an adjacent player. Additionally, strictly when a 7 is rolled, any player holding more than seven resource cards is forced to discard half of their hand; essentially, the game actively penalizes resource hoarding.
Victory Conditions

The winning condition is based on victory points (VPs). Each settlement is worth 1 VP, and each city is worth 2 VPs. Furthermore, constructing a continuous route of at least 5 roads grants the "Longest Road" card, while playing at least 3 Knight cards awards the "Largest Army" card. It is crucial to keep an eye on these cards, each worth 2 VPs, because losing your record means losing the card itself, which can instantly create a 4-point swing between you and a rival. The first player to reach 10 points wins the game.
Development Cards

Finally, development cards allow players to execute special actions. The deck consists of cards that support other game mechanics: progress cards that let you take resources from the bank or build free roads, Knight cards that allow you to move the robber, and direct VP cards. While buying them is not strictly mandatory, they hold significant strategic value and can drastically alter the course of the game.
Technology (Components)
Catan’s map is constructed from hard cardboard hexagonal terrain tiles and a perimeter frame depicting the ocean and harbors.

From what I have observed, the settlement, road, city, and robber figures were made of plastic in earlier editions, whereas newer iterations utilize a wood-like material. The resource and development cards are printed on glossy paper, while the Longest Road, Largest Army, and building cost cards are printed on thicker, more durable cardstock.

When comparing the components of older and newer versions, there is a noticeable progression in both design and material quality; this inadvertently highlights the manufacturing limitations board games faced in the past. Lastly, the dice, perhaps the most critical and entirely unchanged components, continue to drive the game's core system of probability and randomness.
Project Overview: Miracle: Board and Game (MBnG)
Genre: 1-6 Player Cooperative Board Game / Tabletop RPG

The Design Challenge: Streamlining the complex mechanics of traditional Dungeons & Dragons into an accessible, physical grid-based board game experience without losing the depth of class building, stat rolling, and tactical combat.

Core Concept: Players roll a d12 to navigate a 13x13 board, clearing enemy tiles to spawn Minibosses. The ultimate goal is to defeat four Minibosses to summon and defeat the final Boss, using positioning, risk-taking, and macro-resource management.
Spatial Co-op: The "Row Combat" System
To solve the common tabletop issue of "player downtime," combat in MBnG is highly dynamic and position-dependent.

Dynamic Encounters: When a player lands on an Enemy Tile and initiates combat, all other players currently located on that same row (excluding corners) are instantly pulled into the fight cooperatively.

Design Impact: This forces players to strategically coordinate their movement and positioning across the 13x13 grid, ensuring the party stays in formation to support each other during difficult encounters.
The Macro-Economy: Building an Army
Progression is not limited to personal character stats; players must also manage a macro-level resource.
The Soldier Mechanic: Winning battles and completing specific tiles rewards the party with "soldiers" based on the tile's difficulty.

The Boss Nerf: These soldiers act as a collective army. At the start of the final Boss fight, the Boss's total health is mathematically reduced by the accumulated number of soldiers collected by the players throughout the level. This mechanic cleverly incentivizes exploration and combat over rushing the end-game.
Push-Your-Luck Loot System
Looting involves a high-stakes "Push-Your-Luck" mechanic tied directly to player attributes.
Charisma-Based Upgrades: When acquiring an item, a player can attempt to upgrade its rarity (from Common up to Mythical) by rolling a d20 and adding their Charisma modifier.

The Gambler's Ruin: If the player succeeds, they can keep pushing to reach the next tier. However, if they choose to roll and fail at any point, the item is lost completely. This creates intense moments of risk assessment at the table.
Streamlined RPG Depth
Despite the accessible board game format, the combat math retains deep RPG roots.

Stat Integration: Players choose from six classic classes (Warrior, Rogue, Ranger, Wizard, Druid, Cleric) and utilize the standard six attributes (Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma).
Combat Math: Attributes directly scale with specific weapon types, while Constitution combined with armor determines a unit's Armor Class (AC).

Project Overview: Birth of Miracle
Genre: 2.5D Cinematic Puzzle & Adventure
Theme: "The Birth of Curiosity" & "Uncanny Perfection"
My Role: Game Designer & Developer
Inspirations: Limbo, Inside, Little Nightmares
Status: Playable prototype completed, working on additional mechanics to finish VS.
Summary
Overview

Birth of Miracle is a 2.5D narrative platformer with puzzle-solving and light RPG elements,
set in a surreal and metaphysical universe torn apart by divine conflict.

Players follow the journey of the Wanderer, a timeless being who once was a human that discovered the realm of Sanctara; a place beyond time, where knowledge itself shaped existence. Game starts with Wanderer’s arrival to Sanctara and moves through both foundation and destruction of a peaceful commune and the Wanderer’s grief that fractures reality, opening unstable portals that connect countless worlds.

As the player, you traverse through Sanctara, exploring shifting dimensions, solving environmental puzzles, and uncovering the secrets of that holy land. Gameplay combines platforming with exploration-based puzzle design and RPG-style dialogue, mostly monologues, and progression. The player learns new traversal abilities, deciphers ancient symbols, interacts with diverse beings drawn through the portals, and makes narrative choices that alter both the world and the Wanderer’s own nature.

The tone of Birth of Miracle balances philosophical storytelling with tactile, atmospheric
gameplay. Every level acts as both a physical space and a metaphorical journey toward
understanding the “Miracle”; the first act of creation that’s not born from gods, but from human
will.
Core Gameplay Pillars
Birth of Miracle focuses on tactile exploration, symbolic world design, and wordless storytelling where every movement and light source carries narrative intent.
Exploration & Environmental Storytelling: The environment itself “speaks.” The history of Sanctara is revealed through visual cues, murals, and organic remains rather than direct dialogue.
Seamless Puzzle Integration: Puzzles emerge naturally from the environment, mixing timing, logic, and observation without halting the seamless flow of traversal.
Minimalistic Combat Encounters: Short but intense sequences focused on timing, movement, and observation rather than button-mashing.
Light Metroidvania Progression: Unlocking perception-based abilities (e.g., deciphering ancient scripts, manipulating portals) expands exploration in earlier levels without breaking narrative pacing.
The Notebook System (Interactive Lore)
The Wanderer's notes are the player's primary method of understanding the world, placing narrative pacing directly in the player's hands.
The Mechanic: When interacting with specific objects, the Wanderer opens the notebook and starts writing an incomplete observation.
Player Agency: The player makes a choice to fill in the blank. This choice does not alter the main narrative, but dictates the depth and philosophical angle of the lore the player uncovers.

children.text: Gameplay

Birth of Miracle delivers a cinematic 2.5D experience that blends atmospheric platforming,
environmental puzzles, and emotionally charged combat sequences.
Inspired by titles such as Little Nightmares and Inside, the game focuses on tactile
exploration, symbolic world design, and wordless storytelling. Every movement, sound, and
light source carries narrative intent, immersing players in the haunting remnants of Sanctara.
Core Gameplay Pillars

Players traverse the fragmented layers of Sanctara; volcanos, forests, gardens and
surreal dreamscapes.
The environment itself “speaks,” revealing the history of the world through visual
cues, murals, machinery, and organic remains rather than direct dialogue.

Each area features traversal challenges that mix timing, logic, and observation.
The design philosophy prioritizes seamless flow; puzzles emerge naturally from the
environment rather than halting it.

While primarily a puzzle-platformer, the game introduces short but intense combat
sequences.

Combat is minimalistic and deliberate; focused on timing and movement not button-
mashing.

The player unlocks traversal and perception-based abilities: reading ancient scripts,
manipulating energy portals, or momentarily altering reality to solve puzzles or
survive combat.
These upgrades expand exploration possibilities in earlier levels, creating light
Metroidvania loops without breaking narrative pacing.
Narrative Integration

Dialogue is rare and often symbolic; story unfolds through environmental changes,
flashbacks, or brief monologues.
Player decisions; to help, destroy, or ignore, subtly reshape Sanctara’s visual tone and
influence the ending.
Core Gameplay Loop

Explore → Move through interconnected environments, observing and interpreting
symbols.
Solve → Engage with physics-based or logic puzzles integrated into traversal.
Encounter → Face enemies or divine manifestations in controlled combat arenas.

Evolve → Gain new abilities or knowledge that alter both gameplay mechanics and
world state.

Reflect → Return to key sanctuaries or hub areas where the Wanderer records
insights, unlocking narrative layers and opening new portals.
The rhythm of Birth of Miracle alternates between quiet discovery, mechanical challenge,
and philosophical confrontation, maintaining emotional tension throughout the experience.
Level Design for Vertical Slice
The game takes place in Sanctara, in the era before the chaos. Start of the, where the main character, Wanderer, first arrived in the Sanctara.
Art Direction: Flora with golden leaves, white flowers, and endless, radiant light.
Time: There is no concept of time; night never falls, and the player never experiences hunger.
Character: The Wanderer. They have no memory of their past, they do not speak; they only observe and take notes.
The Notebook System
The Wanderer's notes are the player's primary method of understanding the world.
Mechanic: When the player interacts with specific objects, Wanderer opens the notebook and starts writing. The text is left incomplete.
Choice: The player makes a choice to fill in the blank. This choice does not alter the narrative but determines the depth of the lore the player uncovers.
Level Walkthrough

Atmosphere: Dense golden trees, peaceful yet alien.
Awakening & Secret Discovery: The Wanderer spawns in the forest. The camera framing encourages moving right (forward).
If the player moves Left (backward): They find Collectible #1 (The Unfinished Shelter).
Monologue: Pondering why the shelter was abandoned (Insomnia/The absence of passing time).
Tutorial & Lore: The player overcomes basic obstacles (Jumping/Climbing).
Eats a fruit from a tree.
Monologue: The paradox of hunger never subsiding.
Boss Encounter (Erthelian - The Fox): A giant Erthelian blocks the forest exit.
Action: The player navigates through the canopy using stealth to collect a Golden Apple.
Combat: The player must "Dodge" the Fox's attacks. Once the Fox is exhausted, the player climbs onto it and feeds it the apple.
Resolution: The Fox calms down and begins following the player (Follow AI).
image.png
Atmosphere: Wide rivers, open skies, golden bushes.
Tracking: The player finds Collectible #2 (Scorch Mark) on the path.
Monologue: Contemplating the scorching power that passed through here (Fear vs. Curiosity).
Scripted Event: A portal of light opens from a pit (Orthodionois) ahead. An Orthodionos (The Angel) emerges. The Angel drops a piece of paper before ascending into the sky.
Stealth Sequence: The Angel hovers in the air, sweeping the ground with light cones from its eyes. The player proceeds using stealth and retrieves the note.
Monologue: Analyzing the runes on the note.
Reward: The melody required to open the castle gate.

River Crossing / Stamina Mechanic: The river is extremely turbulent. The Wanderer cannot cross alone, but the Fox (bonded via the apple) arrives. The Wanderer rides on the Fox's back. As the Fox resists the current, the Wanderer is tossed about. The player must hold the "Grab" button, draining their stamina. During brief lulls, the player must release the button to regenerate stamina.
Visual Detail: Arthalian (Fish) sentinels can be seen swimming in the water.

Atmosphere: The golden river, gardens.
The Climb: The castle sits on a high embankment. The Fox provides a final boost, throwing the Wanderer onto a platform, and stays behind.
Monologue: Noting that the river flowing here is golden (Sanctariis).

Hazard (Urthulian - The Owl): As the Wanderer climbs the wall, a patrolling Urthulian (Owl) appears in the air. If the Owl strikes, the Wanderer loses their grip and falls to the bottom of the embankment, forcing a re-climb.
Exploration: Collectible #3 (Angel Feather) is found on a ledge during the climb.
image.png
Atmosphere: A magnificent gothic gate, absolute silence.

Audio Puzzle: The gate is locked. In front of it are Sanctaryst Crystals of varying sizes. The wind whispers a melody; the player deciphers which runes correspond to this melody using the previously acquired note. The player strikes the crystals in the correct sequence to mimic the melody.
Ending: The gate opens. White light pours out from within. The Wanderer steps inside. Fade to black.
Story

In an unknown time, from an unknown universe, on an unknown planet inhabited by an
unknown race, someone notices a brilliant, glowing white light in a distant corner. Driven by
curiosity, they approach the source of the light and find a door. The door stands wide open,
and dazzling light pours from within. Stepping through that door changes the destiny of the
man we now call Wanderer forever.

After passing through the door, the Wanderer finds himself in an entirely different place.
Overcoming his initial shock, he tries to return to where he came from, only to discover that
the portal has vanished. Alone in this mysterious place with no knowledge of his
surroundings, he must survive. When he searches for food, he quickly finds icy, clear streams
and delicious fruits, unlike anything he has ever tasted. However, a peculiar realization dawns
on him: although he gathers food and water into his backpack, he never feels hunger or thirst,
despite hours, perhaps even days, passing. Then again, days cannot pass, for it has never grown dark since his arrival. Thinking he may be losing his mind, the Wanderer builds a small
shelter with materials from his surroundings to rest, but he cannot sleep either.
Spending a long time in this strange place, the Wanderer eventually concludes that he is in
what we might call Eden. Here, there is no hunger, thirst, or sleep, and he tires far less than
normal. With no better task at hand, he begins to explore, taking notes and drawing maps of
the realm in the notebook he had brought with him.

One of the most important observations he records is that Eden exists outside the concept of
time, he cannot tell how long he has been there, though his consciousness feels as if years
have passed. He also theorizes that this place is not a physical planet within any observable
universe. On his travels, he encounters only three living beings: a fox-like, an owl-like, and a
salmon-like creature, all unconscious and non-aggressive, aimlessly wandering the landscape.
The plants, with golden leaves and white blossoms, and the golden trees are unlike anything
in the world he knew. Yet, this place has one more remarkable encounter in store that will
change everything.

From his maps, the Wanderer discovers that the terrain of Eden is divided into sharply distinct
regions. The entire realm is a perfect circle, with a massive structure at its centre. Streams
radiate outward from the centre toward the perimeter, interspersed with lakes and waterfalls at regular intervals. The landscape descends from the centre outward in a series of levels:
volcanoes at the outermost edge, followed by rocky mountains, forests, meadows, valleys, and gardens, until finally, the Sanctarium lies at the very heart. The Sanctarium is unique to Eden, containing rare minerals, golden water springs, magnificent trees, a sky of pure white, and a massive castle resembling Gothic architecture. Though the Wanderer is deeply curious about what lies within the Sanctarium Castle, he never could find the courage to enter, frightened by the thought of he might bother someone in there and get caught.

Despite the symmetry and order of the terrain, he finds random large pits across the
landscape. These pits are wide but shallow, and symbols incomprehensible to him are carved
into their floors. One day, while walking near a pit, a white light suddenly appears in its
centre, the same light that brought him here. Excited by the thought of returning home, the
Wanderer rushes toward the portal but stops as he notices something emerging from it.
Out of the portal come huge, six-eyed, six-armed beings with glowing skin like sunlight and
six wings flowing like silk behind them. Frightened, Wanderer hides behind a tree and
watches. The beings begin to fly in another direction, and just before taking off, one of them
drops a piece of paper. Once they disappear and the portal closes, Wanderer, ensuring his
safety, descends into the pit to retrieve the paper. On the paper there are symbols resembling those engraved on the pit floor. At that moment, he realizes it is time to face his fears and enter the Sanctarium Castle.

On his way to the castle, the Wanderer neither sees the creatures again nor encounters any
obstacles. The castle doors are open, and he walks freely inside. Despite its immense size, the
castle is mostly empty, bare rooms, gardens, fountains, and grand halls. Distracted by its
beauty, he forgets his mission until he finds himself before a locked door. Determined to learn more about the creatures, the language he cannot read, and the mysteries of this place, he begins mapping the castle, searching for a window or another way to access the room.
After what feels like years of effort, he finds no alternative entrance. He tries to force the door
open many times, but it remains immovable. According to his maps, there should be nothing
but a tiny space behind it. Despite living comfortably in the castle, his relentless curiosity
tears him apart.

One day, while sitting in a desk studying his plans, he hears a noise. Peeking into the hallway,
he sees the locked door shining with blinding light before it vanishes. Heart racing, he
watches as one of the terrifying creatures’steps through the now-open doorway into another
room. As soon as it disappears, he quietly approaches the door. Inside, just as his map predicted, is a small marble chamber, its walls smooth and white. Again, there are some symbols carved on the floor. As he was checking them, the floor beneath him suddenly descends. Terrified, he keeps his eyes shut until the movement stops. When he opens his eyes, he finds himself in a vast library. Realizing the importance of this discovery, the Wanderer decides to stay and study, though he knows the creature might return at any moment. Testing the floor mechanism, he successfully sends it back up and hides behind a nearby shelf. Sure enough, another creature soon arrives. Somehow, Wanderer senses this is a different one. Without looking around, it walks straight into the depths of the library and vanishes from sight. For a long time, the Wanderer roams the library freely. He explores endless shelves, trying to decipher the writings but with little success. Then, he stumbles upon a book in his own language, a novel he had read in his world. Examining the surrounding shelves, he realizes they contain thousands of books; maybe even copies of every book ever written. As excited as he can be, he immerses himself in reading for what feels like an eternity. Among the countless volumes, he discovers a collection of books written in the same symbols carved into the floor. Over years, perhaps lifetimes, he translates and studies them, filling notebooks with his findings. Isolated from the golden fruits and clear streams, with no pleasures but knowledge, he learns more about the creatures and the world than they themselves may know.

Eventually, wearied by solitude and overwhelmed by the weight of his discoveries, the
Wanderer grows tired. He returns to the platform that had brought him down, waiting for the
next guard change to slip back out as silently as he came. At last, when the moment comes, he ascends, drinks deeply from the nearest stream and eats golden apples as much as he can,
even though he is neither thirsty nor hungry. And when he feels satisfied, he begins his next
quest, to build a community in this realm, armed with the knowledge that only he possesses.
From the endless library, he had learned the sacred art of opening portals; bridges between
worlds and times. Yet, he had long forgotten where he came from. His world, his name, his
people; all lost to eternity. Thus, out of longing rather than purpose, he began opening small gateways to distant realms. Through them, he met others; wanderers like himself, seekers, scholars, and dreamers from countless worlds. He spoke many tongues, and his words carried a strange calmness that drew hearts together. Slowly, they gathered around him, those who wished to learn. And so, upon the shores of a golden lake, the First Commune of Sanctara was born. It was a quiet, harmonious place. They built a small town, shared songs from worlds long dead, and studied under the endless white sky. The Wanderer taught them what he had learned; not only about portals, but about thought, creation, and the language of existence itself. For a time, peace seemed eternal. But eternity is never silent for long.

Far beyond Sanctara’s heavens, the One they called the Creator, God himself, had been watching. Perhaps the solitary Wanderer had gone unnoticed; a single flicker in an infinite void. Yet now, a fire burned where only stillness should reign. Life; mortal, flawed, and self-aware; had taken root within the sacred realm.

And so, the Orthodionos, God’s soldiers, descended. Commune tried to hold their ground for a while; their knowledge was what made them powerful. But soon enough, one day when Wanderer was at a distant realm, their wings of light tore the sky apart as they brought fire upon the Commune. No plea, no resistance, no mercy; only divine silence. The golden gardens turned to ash; the streams boiled to mist. When the Wanderer returned, he found nothing; no voices, no songs, only the empty echoes of what he had created. Something within him broke. For the first time since stepping through the first door, he felt rage; pure and endless. He cast his maps to the wind, shattered the sacred stones, and called upon the knowledge he had once again.
And the sky answered.

Portals erupted across Sanctara, uncontrolled, eternal. Through them came countless beings;
mortals and monsters, all kinds of creatures, all drawn to the same grief, the same fury.
Realities began to bleed together; worlds collided and merged into chaos. The Orthodionos
returned to silence the storm, but the storm had no center anymore. Every portal brough
different life-forms to Sanctara and soon they started fighting with both each other and the
God. And from that day, Sanctara was no longer Eden. It became a wound across existence; the birthplace of both creation and rebellion. The Birth of Miracle.

Project Overview: Miracle: Born and Dead (MBaD)
Genre: Turn-Based Strategy / Real-Time Tactics (RTT)
The Design Challenge: Bridging the gap between grand strategic empire management and micro-level real-time tactical combat within a deeply asymmetric, multi-faction original IP.

Core Concept: A dual-phase strategy game where players guide an Industrial Age human army across the metaphysical realm of Eden. Players must manage resources, outposts, and exploration in a simultaneous turn-based "Camp Phase," and seamlessly transition into commanding large-scale armies in an isometric, real-time "Battle Phase".
The Macro Layer: Simultaneous Turn Execution
To maintain pacing and heighten strategic tension, the global map (Camp Phase) abandons traditional sequential turns.

Simultaneous Resolution: Players allocate tasks—such as sending Explorers, upgrading Outposts, or moving troops—but no actions occur until the "Ready" phase is triggered. Once triggered, all player and enemy actions resolve simultaneously.

Dynamic Encounter System: Because movement occurs at the same time, military encounters are highly unpredictable. Intersecting paths can result in different engagement types, including Pitched Battles, Outpost Sieges, or Ambushes, depending on intelligence gathered by Explorers.
The Micro Layer: Tactical Real-Time Combat
When armies clash, the game shifts to a real-time isometric battlefield where positioning, terrain, and unit synergy dictate the outcome.
Advanced Unit Control: Players command troops using a system heavily inspired by Mount and Blade, utilizing keyword mappings to order entire unit classes or individually selecting specific squads.

Environmental Tactics: The battlefield features heavily impactful terrain modifiers. For instance, Lava tiles are completely impassable to most factions, but gravity-controlling Graphons and alchemist Zemihkes can traverse them.
Asymmetric Faction & Unit Design
The game features five deeply asymmetric main factions (Humans, telepathic Klimarans, gravity-shifting Graphons, alchemist Zemihkes, and divine Orthodionos) with specialized unit archetypes.
Dynamic Riders: Cavalry units can actively mount and dismount mid-battle, swapping between high-mobility heavy combatants and standard close-range infantry as the tactical situation demands.
Combat Engineers: Engineer units dynamically reshape the battlefield in real-time by constructing trenches, ladders, and siege towers, or by building bridges over impassable water and lava terrains.

Assassins & Traps: Stealth units can utilize specific environments (like bushes or forests) to hide from the enemy AI, gaining damage multipliers on their next strike or laying down proximity traps with varying setup times.
Progression & Objective System
Progression is tied to an invisible, organic objective system rather than a linear quest log.

Hidden Milestones: Similar to Souls-like narrative design, even though it is unusual for a strategy game, objectives are entirely optional and discovered organically through exploration or post-battle clues.

Tiered Economy: The economy is driven by a six-tier resource system (Wood, Stone, Steel, Arfashiler, Fharaber, Sanctaryst) that requires constant map expansion and territorial control to fuel high-level outpost construction and specialized troop formations.

Project Overview: Harvey Park
Genre: Psychological Horror / Anomaly Detection
Team: Boiler Works (Team of four)
My Role: Game Designer, Developer, Narrative Designer
Core Concept: Set in a futuristic mining tower, players must observe rooms, restore power, and make life-or-death decisions in an elevator to escape an ancient entity named Echo.
The Elevator Loop: Observation & Judgment
The core gameplay relies on memory, attention to detail, and decision-making under intense psychological pressure.

Two-Phase Observation: When players enter a floor, it is illuminated only by Echo's external light, forcing them to memorize the room's normal state. Upon repairing the power switch, internal lights activate, and there is a 50% chance an anomaly has been triggered.
The Elevator Decision: To progress, players must return to the elevator and choose between "Anomaly Present" or "No Anomaly".

Roguelike Consequences: A correct decision moves the player up one floor and grants extra time to the hidden clock. A wrong decision drops the player down a floor and resets the anomaly state, increasing the pressure.
The "Echo" Threat System
Combat is non-existent; the game uses a dual-threat system to create constant tension and prevent players from taking unlimited time.

Red Echo (The Hidden Timer): A 5-minute hidden timer that follows Harvey from below. As time runs out, the player experiences screen darkening, whispers, and heavy breathing. If the timer reaches zero, Red Echo catches Harvey and resets the entire run to the bottom floor.

White Echo (The Direct Pursuer): White Echo circles outside the tower, providing eerie illumination. If the player takes too long on a floor, it enters the room and begins a direct chase, but it stops moving when the player looks directly at it.
Level Progression & Spatial Puzzles
The tower consists of 16 distinct floors, transitioning from clean, functional sci-fi environments to corrupted, blood-stained nightmares.
Anomaly Categories: The game features "Spatial Anomalies" (changes in object size, location, or number) and "Story Anomalies" (objects from Harvey's past that don't belong in a sci-fi tower).

The Final Boss (Fusion Room): The top floor features a corrupted room that physically manifests Echo. This room fuses props from all previous levels (e.g., Medical Bay gurneys wrapped in Greenhouse vines), creating the ultimate memory test where players must recall the entire journey.

Project Overview
Genre: Roguelike Dungeon Crawler / Card Game
Core Mechanic: Resource management and risk assessment with a deck of playing cards, where each suit is a verb and the weapon degrades to whatever it last killed.

Concept

Dekrawler is a single-player roguelike dungeon crawler played entirely with a deck of playing cards. One run is one deck: you draw four cards into a room, resolve them, and move on. Clear every threat in the deck and you win. It builds on the core loop of Scoundrel and its central tension, a weapon that degrades as it kills, and adds a run-to-run meta layer, a thirteen-tier campaign and two additional suits.
Summary
The 52-Card Dungeon (Core Loop)

The game is played in rooms of four cards. You resolve enough of them that one or fewer is left, then you may leave, and the leftovers carry into the next room. Ranks 2 to 10 are their number, J is 11, Q is 12, K is 13 and A is 14. Beyond the four standard suits, Oracle reveals and rearranges part of the deck, and Python hides its face until it is played.

content.text: Signature Systems & Mechanics
Weapon Degradation System

Weapons do not simply break, they dynamically scale down. Equip a Diamond and its rank is your weapon power. Kill a Club with it and the weapon locks to that Club's rank, so from then on it can only be used on Clubs of that rank or lower.
• Example: killing a Club 7 with a Diamond 10 locks the weapon at 7.
This is the whole game. Kill the weakest Club first and your weapon is locked at the bottom, so every Club above it has to be fought barehanded. Kill the strongest first and the ceiling stays high.
The Adrenaline (Combo) Economy
To incentivize aggressive sequencing, Gold generation requires chaining kills of the same target type. The payout multiplier escalates linearly after the 3rd consecutive kill, calculated as:
M = max(1, n - 2)
(Where “n” is the consecutive kill streak. Equipping a new weapon, healing, or switching targets immediately resets the combo to zero).
Balancing & Testing (Monte Carlo Simulations)

Balance is measured rather than estimated. The simulator drives the real game engine instead of a separate model of it, so a reading cannot drift from the shipped rules.
• Automated simulations: thousands of runs per tier under a scripted policy, reporting clear rates for the bare campaign and for a fully invested loadout.
• Iterative tuning: the campaign ladder is authored as rules rather than numbers, and each rule is introduced on its own before it is combined with another.

Core Loop

children.text: The Objective
You are navigating a dangerous dungeon using a standard 52-card deck. Your goal is to survive the entire deck without your Health Points (HP) dropping to zero. You start with 20 Max HP.
The Room (Turn Structure)

The game is played in "Rooms". At the start of each turn, you draw 4 cards from the deck and place them face-up on the board. You must interact with these cards strategically. Once you have cleared the board (or decided to leave the remaining cards behind), you draw the next 4 cards to enter the next Room. You may leave the room either when there are no more cards left or only one card is left.
The Suits & Mechanics

Each suit in the deck represents a different element of the dungeon:
• ♦️ Diamonds (Weapons): These are your tools for survival. You can equip a Diamond as a weapon to fight enemies. You can only hold one weapon at a time. If you pick up a new Diamond, your currently equipped weapon is discarded.
• ♥️ Hearts (Health Potions): Drinking a Heart restores your HP by the card's face value. Your HP cannot exceed your maximum limit.
• ♣️ Clubs (Elite Enemies): These are the main monsters. To defeat a Club, you must use your equipped Weapon.
    ◦ If your Weapon's value is greater than or equal to the Enemy's value, you defeat it and take 0 damage.
    ◦ If your Weapon is weaker than the Enemy (or if you are unarmed), you take damage equal to the difference. (e.g., If you have a 5 Weapon and attack a 9 Enemy, you take 4 damage).
• ♠️ Spades (Pests/Hazards): These are swarming hazards. They work differently than Clubs:
    ◦ Any weapon equipped (no matter what its degrated value is) can be used against Spades with its full face value, but you still take the exceed damage. You cannot clear a spade without a weapon. Clearing spades does not degrade the weapon.
    ◦ If you choose not to clear a Spade andl leave the room, for every Spade left on the board when you draw the next 3 cards, you take 1 direct damage. Every time you leave the room with a Spade left, next damage you take from Spades increases by one.
End of the Run

The loop continues: draw 4 cards, manage your weapon degradation, clear pests, build combos, and survive. If your HP hits 0, the run ends. If you clear the deck, you proceed to the next, more challenging level!

content.text: Mechanics and Systems

children.text: Deterministic Values

The numerical value of each card strictly dictates its mechanical weight (e.g., an enemy's HP, a weapon's durability, or a potion's healing yield). This creates a tightly bound, predictable scaling system:
Numbered Cards (2-10): Face value.
Face/Court Cards: Jack (11), Queen (12), King (13), Ace (14).

Design Perspective: Capping the maximum value at 14 ensures that the mathematical bounds remain manageable. It allows the player to calculate exact survival odds without the frustration of infinite numerical inflation.
Fleeing System
There are two types of fleeing: classical flee and desperation flee.

• Classical Flee: You can flee a room if you haven’t interacted with any of the four cards dealt. If you flee, all cards in the room are sent to the downside of the deck. You take no damage from spades. You cannot use classical flee in two rooms in a row.

• Desperation Flee: You can flee a room if you haven’t interacted with any of the four cards dealt, just like classical flee. But this time, if you flee, only black cards in the room are sent to the downside of the deck and red cards are discarded. You take damage from sent spades. But you can use desperation flee any time you want.
Weapon Degredation System

This is the heart of the game's strategy. Weapons do not break after a single use, but they degrade. When you defeat a Club enemy, your Weapon's maximum power drops to match the value of the enemy you just killed.
• Example: You equip a Diamond 10. You attack and kill a Club 7. You take no damage, but your weapon's power is now reduced to 7. You can no longer kill an 8-value enemy without taking damage.
• Note: Clearing Spades (Pests) does not degrade your weapon.
Adrenaline (Combo) System
To incentivize aggressive sequencing and punish overly passive play, Gold generation is governed by a progressive combo multiplier based on consecutive enemy (Clubs) kills.
Killing the same type of target consecutively (e.g., Club-Club, or Spade-Spade) increases your Combo Multiplier.
The Gold you earn equals the defeated enemy's value multiplied by your current Combo.

Combo Breaker: Equipping a new Weapon (Diamond), drinking a Potion (Heart), or switching your target type (Clubs-Spade) immediately resets your combo to zero. You must balance your greed for Gold with your need to heal and upgrade your weapons.
Multiplier
Kills 1 to 3: Standard yield (x1 Multiplier). The baseline economy is tight.
Kill 4 and beyond: Linear escalation. The 4th consecutive kill grants a x2 multiplier, the 5th grants x3, the 6th grants x4, and so forth.
Multiplier Formula: For a consecutive kill streak of n, the payout multiplier M is calculated as M = max(1, n - 2).

Design Perspective: This structure forces players to strategically manipulate the board state. Leaving weaker enemies alive to build a larger combo chain becomes a calculated risk, adding immense depth to the resource management loop.
In-Game Economy & Meta-Progression
The game features a dual-currency system designed to balance short-term risk assessment during a run with long-term strategic investment in the meta-game.
1. Run Currency: Gold

Gold is the volatile, in-run currency. It dictates your purchasing power during a single attempt and resets when you die or complete a run.
• Acquisition (The Adrenaline System): Gold is generated primarily by defeating Clubs (Enemies). The base payout is equal to the face value of the defeated Club.
• Combo Multiplier: Chaining kills of the same target type (e.g., Club-Club or Spade-Spade) increases the Combo Multiplier (x1, x2, x3...). The total Gold earned is the card's value multiplied by the current combo.
• Combo Breakers: Equipping a new Diamond (Weapon), using a Heart (Potion), or switching the target type immediately resets the multiplier back to zero.
• The Shop: Every 4 cleared rooms, the player enters a safe zone containing a Shop. Here, Gold is spent on single-use consumables, temporary buffs, and run-specific passive items.
2. Meta Currency: Soul Crystals

Soul Crystals are the permanent, hard currency of the game. They are never lost upon death and are used exclusively in the main menu to expand the player's arsenal.
• Acquisition Methods:
◦ End-of-Run Conversion: When a run ends (victory or death), all accumulated Gold is liquidated into Crystals at a fixed exchange rate (e.g., 100 Gold = 1 Crystal).
◦ Boss Bounties: Defeating the highest value targets, specifically the Ace of Clubs and Ace of Spades, grants an immediate +1 Crystal bounty.
◦ Adrenaline Rush: Reaching a Combo Multiplier of x8 or higher rewards the player with +1 Crystal for every subsequent consecutive kill in that chain.
• Meta-Progression Sinks (The Mystic Shop):
◦ Campaign Unlocks: Spending Crystals to unlock the next deck tier (increasing difficulty modifiers and rulesets).
◦ Permanent Artifacts: Purchasing passive buffs that are equipped before a run begins (e.g., starting with extra Max HP or a base weapon).
◦ The Joker Forge (Gacha & Merge): Crystals are used to pull random "Joker" cards from a depleting pool to shuffle into the run deck. Players can also pay a hefty Crystal fee to merge three identical Joker cards into a single "Golden Joker" with doubled effects.

content.text: Progression

children.text: Overview

The game features an 8-tier Campaign mode. Instead of a single endless run, players must conquer increasingly difficult versions of the dungeon. Each tier introduces severe mathematical disadvantages, forcing the player to rely on their meta-progression (Artifacts and Golden Jokers) and strategic deck-building to survive.
Unlock System
Players do not automatically progress to the next difficulty upon winning. To unlock a new Deck Tier, two strict conditions must be met:
Completion: The player must successfully survive and complete the immediately preceding Deck Tier at least once.

Crystal Payment: The player must pay a one-time unlock fee using Soul Crystals at the Mystic Shop. This creates a natural loop where players must "farm" lower tiers to afford the entry fee for higher tiers.

Spades are +3 Value. Requires significantly stronger weapons just to clear pests without taking the snowballing damage penalty.
Diamonds are -2 Value. Weapons are inherently weaker. Impossible to kill King Clubs without taking damage unless buffed.
Face Clubs (J, Q, K) deal x2 Damage. Punishes unarmed players and weak weapons with lethal burst damage.

All negative modifiers combined. (Spades +3, Diamonds -2, Clubs x1.5). The ultimate Grandmaster test. Requires a mathematically perfect loadout to survive.

children.text: Meta-Progression: Permanent Artifacts
Overview

Permanent Artifacts are powerful passive modifiers purchased with Soul Crystals in the main menu's Mystic Shop. Unlike in-run Shop items, which are temporary and lost upon death or completion, Artifacts form the player's core arsenal and remain active for the entirety of the run.
Loadout System
To maintain game balance and prevent the player from mathematically outscaling the deck too quickly, Artifacts are governed by a strict slot system.
Base Capacity: The player begins the game with only 1 active Artifact slot.
Upgrading Capacity: Players can spend a significant amount of Soul Crystals to permanently unlock additional slots (e.g., expanding to a maximum of 3 slots).

Strategic Build-Crafting: Before embarking on a run, the player must select and equip their Artifacts from their unlocked collection. This forces strategic decision-making based on the selected Deck Tier. (e.g., Equipping economy-focused Artifacts to farm Gold on lower tiers, or prioritizing heavy combat modifiers to survive the "Apocalypse" tier).
Artifact Categories & Pricing
Artifacts are priced according to their tier and how deeply they alter the mathematical deficit of the run. Here are the artifacts tiers with a few example artifacts:
Tier 1 - Fundamentals (50 Crystal): Basic utility and early-game safety nets.
Apprentice Badge: Begin the run with a Diamond 4 (Weapon) already equipped, preventing early unarmed damage.
Inheritance: Start the run with 25 Gold in your pocket.
Tier 2 - Sustain & Economy (200 Crystal): Modifiers that ease the core loop constraints and resource management.
Vampire Tooth: Recover 1 HP for every 5 enemies defeated.
Leather Scabbard: Weapons degrade slower (e.g., absorbing 1 point of degradation per kill).
Combo Apprentice: The Adrenaline (Combo) Multiplier starts at x2 instead of x1.
Tier 3 - Game Changers (500 Crystal): Expensive investments that drastically alter combat calculus or break standard rules.
Adrenaline: Weapons face value x2 damage when the player's HP drops below 20%.
Stainless Steel: Clearing Spades (Pests) provides heals 2 HP.
Titan's Grip: Face value of Jack, Queen, King and Ace of Diamonds are increased by 2.
Jokers and The Forge
Overview

Jokers are powerful, rule-breaking cards that are physically shuffled into the run deck. Unlike standard suit cards, Jokers provide unique tactical advantages ranging from direct damage and healing to deck manipulation and economic boosts. To acquire them, players must engage with a randomized Gacha system using Soul Crystals and manage their duplicates strategically.
Acquisition
Players purchase new Jokers from the main menu using their hard-earned Soul Crystals. The system allows for infinite duplicates, encouraging players to hoard identical cards for future upgrades.
Single Pull: 20 Crystal
Triple Pull Bundle: 50 Crystal (A discounted bundle saving 10 Crystals, encouraging bulk purchases)
Rarity & Drop Rates
The Joker pool consists of 50 unique cards divided into four distinct rarity tiers. The probability of pulling a card is strictly tied to its rarity:
Common (50% Drop Rate): Fundamental utility cards (e.g., The Thief - steals 20 Gold, Healing Fairy - restores 5 HP).
Rare (30% Drop Rate): Tactical board-control cards (e.g., The Bomb - deals 10 AoE damage, The Freezer - delays enemy attacks).
Epic (15% Drop Rate): Run-saving interventions (e.g., The Fool - acts as a wildcard, Holy Light - clears all Spades instantly).
Legendary (5% Drop Rate): Game-breaking phenomenons (e.g., Time Stop - grants free attacks, Exodia Piece - an alternate win condition).
The Forge (Merging Duplicate Jokers)

Drawing duplicates is not a punishment; it is the core of the late-game progression. Inspired by auto-battler mechanics, players can access "The Forge" to combine their duplicate Jokers into ultimate versions of themselves.
The Merge Formula: 3x Identical Base Jokers + Crystal Fee = 1x Golden Joker
The Golden Effect: A Golden Joker yields exactly 2x the power, efficiency, or trigger rate of its base counterpart.

Slot Efficiency: A Golden Joker takes up only one card slot in the deck while providing the value of two, allowing players to mathematically out-scale the higher difficulties without bloating their deck size.
Merge Costs
Merging requires a significant Crystal investment based on the card's rarity, creating a massive long-term goal for dedicated players.

content.text: Balancing & Testing Methodology

children.text: Theoretical Framework

Currently, the numerical values for the meta-progression economy (crystal costs, joker drop rates, tier modifiers, etc.) represent a baseline mathematical model. These default values were established using standard exponential progression curves to create a robust "paper prototype". The goal of this phase is to ensure the core economic loop is logically sound on paper before hardcoding values into the engine.
Planned Simulation & Empirical Testing (Current State)

Moving from theoretical balance to empirical data is the next critical step. To refine these default numbers, I am currently working on building a lightweight script in Python to run automated Monte Carlo simulations of the game.

Running thousands of simulated hands will allow me to build a well-balanced in-game economy. Based on this data, the earning and cost values will be iteratively adjusted to ensure the late-game remains punishingly difficult but mathematically solvable.

content.text: Platform & Controls

children.text: The game is designed for cross-platform accessibility, targeting both PC and Mobile. The control scheme is highly tactile and minimalist, utilizing intuitive drag-and-drop mechanics for PC (mouse) and fluid swipe gestures for Mobile platforms.

content.text: Art Direction

children.text: To maintain absolute focus on the core mathematical loop and strategic decision-making, the UI is strictly card-centric. Similar to Balatro, there are no character avatars, excessive animations, or overly flashy visual effects to distract the player.

However, rather than a bright casino aesthetic, the visual direction leans into a dark, atmospheric dungeon crawler vibe. Drawing inspiration from the grim, tactile nature of Inscryption and the distinct, moody art styles of Slay the Spire, the aesthetic relies on subtle, shadowy environments and highly readable card art to convey the mechanical weight and danger of the dungeon.

Unfortuanetly as I am not a visual artist myself, I will either be working on my own skillts to bring my visual vision for this game to life or seek out help from other visual artists. I do not intend to use any AI generated content for any of the projects I work on.

content.text: Project Overview: Moods of İstanbul
Genre: Scalable Civic Negotiation / Semi-Cooperative Board Game
Role: Game Designer

The Design Challenge: Creating a highly modular "Megagame" system where the physical play area and player count dynamically expand (from 4 to 8 to 16+ players), simulating the escalating complexity of urban planning and bureaucracy.

Core Concept: Players take on distinct civic roles (Student, Retiree, etc.) and draft personal problem cards. They must negotiate under a strict time limit to pass "Policies" that satisfy their faction's needs while aligning with the harsh statistical realities of the city.
Tabletop Link: https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3617223490
Note: Visuals provided were not created by myself.
Rulebook

children.text: SECTION 1: Setup and Problem Detection
Table Layout and Team

Game Area: Each table represents a 1km^2 area of Istanbul.
• Player Count: The game is played with total players in multiples of 4 (4, 8,
16...).
• Seating: Exactly 4 players sit at the table, with one player positioned at each
side of the square.
• Mission: Initially, you are responsible only for your own area.
Roles and Personal Problems

Starting Status: Everyone begins with 0 IPA Points.
• Role Card: Each player draws a Role Card (e.g., Student, Retiree).
• Problem Selection: From a deck of 100 cards, each player selects 5 Problem
Cards based on their own priorities.
• Current State: There are now a total of 20 Different Problem Cards on the
table waiting for solutions.
Facing Reality (IPA Data Card)

Critical Moment: Immediately after problems are selected, reveal 1 IPA Data
Card for that square.
• Awareness Test: This card shows the statistical reality of the area (e.g.,
"Green space per person is 1m2").
• Question: Do your 20 problems align with this scientific fact? (This card
guides your solution choices!)
• Important Note: The IPA Data Card is available only in the first and last
round of the game.
SECTION 2: Solution Generation
Creating the Solution Package (20 Solutions)

Now, everyone acts as a planner.
• Task: Each player prepares 5 Solution Cards that address their 5 problems or
the IPA Data Card.
• Resources: You can select from the pre-made Solution Deck or take a Wild
Card to write your own unique solution (e.g., 3 Pre-made + 2 Wild Cards).
Wild Card

Players should write down benefical roles and problem solved
information on the Wild Card as well as how to solve that problem while
creating the Wild Card. This is important as this information will decide which
players will gain IPA points from that Wild Card.
• Result: Before negotiation begins, a total of 20 Solution Cards have
accumulated on the table.
SECTION 3: Negotiation and Decision
The Grand Negotiation

• This is the most critical phase. There are 20 proposed solutions, but our
budget/time only allows for 4 Policies.
• Time Limit: 10 Minutes [Subject to revision].
• Process: The group discusses, eliminates 16 cards, and selects the 4 Final
Policies to implement.
• Strategy: You must choose cards that cover the IPA data and address the
problems of everyone in the group.
SECTION 4: Scoring and Results
Score Calculation (N=Round Number)

Everyone calculates their score using this formula:
• Role Impact: If a chosen policy fits your Role: +2N Points.
• Problem Resolution: If a chosen policy solves one of your 5 Personal Problems:
+4N Points.
• IPA Data Match: If a chosen card matches the IPA Data Card on the table, the
player who brought that card gains +6*N Point.
Wild Card Bonus

If a Wild Card written by a player is included in the final 4 policies; the player
who first proposed/wrote that idea earns an extra +6*N Points for their
creativity.
SECTION 5: Progression and Finale
Merging

At the end of the round, each table physically merges with a random
neighboring table.

Two 4-player tables become an 8-player council. The area expands to
2km^2 and doubles each turn.
• The process repeats in the new round (New problems, new solutions), but
now a larger group negotiates.
Winning Condition

At the end of the game, each player calculates their total IPA points,
including the points from the solution cards selected in the last round.
• All players with the same Role form a group and their points together
• Each Role group must have a minimum total score of 6N(number of
players in the group)
• If this minimum is achieved, all players in that Role group win; if not, they
lose.
• There is no restriction on multiple Role groups winning simultaneously,
but one group accumulating too many points might prevent other groups
from earning enough points.

content.text: Dynamic Scaling: The "Merging" Mechanic
The standout technical feature of Moods of İstanbul is its physical modularity. The game does not take place on a static board.

Bureaucratic Expansion: The game starts at isolated tables of 4 players, representing a 1km² local district. At the end of a round, tables physically merge. Two 4-player tables combine into an 8-player council, expanding the map to 2km².

Design Impact: As the game progresses, the player count and the board size double. This brilliantly mimics urban sprawl and the increasing difficulty of reaching a consensus in larger political bodies. A negotiation strategy that worked with 4 people will completely break down in a room of 16, forcing players to constantly adapt their social dynamics.
The Bottleneck: Subjective Desires vs. Objective Reality
The core gameplay loop revolves around high-tension resource scarcity and time-boxed diplomacy.

The Reality Check (IPA Data Card): Before proposing solutions, an "IPA Data Card" is revealed, showing real-world statistical data of the district (e.g., "Green space per person is 1m²"). This acts as an anchor, forcing players to align their subjective role-playing goals with objective scientific facts to maximize points.

The 10-Minute Diplomacy: In the Solution Phase, 20 different proposed Solution Cards (including player-crafted "Wild Cards") are placed on the table. However, the system's "budget" only allows for 4 Final Policies to be implemented. Players have exactly 10 minutes to argue, form alliances, and eliminate 16 cards.
Faction-Based Economy and Win Conditions
Moods of İstanbul employs a semi-cooperative, faction-based scoring system rather than a single-winner format.
Role Synergy: Throughout the game, players earn "IPA Points" based on how well the passed policies impact their specific Role, solve their Personal Problems, or match the IPA Data.

The Faction Threshold: At the end of the game, players do not win individually. All players sharing the same Role (across the massive merged table) pool their points together. To win, a Role faction must cross a mathematical threshold:
6 * N * (Number of players in that faction)

System Balance: Multiple factions can win simultaneously. However, because only 4 policies can be passed per round, if one faction is too greedy and monopolizes the policies, they will inevitably starve the other factions of points, creating a deeply realistic political simulation.
Project Overview: Sown in Silence (Working Title)
Genre: Narrative Adventure / Genre-Blend (Farming Sim + Metroidvania)

The Design Challenge: Effectively juxtaposing the "Cozy" gameplay loops of farming and dating simulators with the existential dread of cosmic horror, creating a gameplay experience that feels both familiar and deeply unsettling.

Core Concept: Players live a dual life: by day, they manage a farm and build relationships in a seemingly peaceful village; by night, they explore an ancient, shifting temple to communicate with a cosmic entity that challenges their reality.
My Role: Concept & System Designer
Inspirations: H.P. Lovecraft Stories, Stardew Valley, Metroid
Dual-Loop Systems: Routine vs. Revelation
The gameplay is structured around two contrasting loops that feed into each other to build narrative and mechanical momentum.

rows: Provides resources and Mental Stability (required to safely explore the temple).
Unlocks narrative revelations and "Forbidden Knowledge" that recontextualizes the day-cycle events.

content.text: Metroidvania Progression: "Knowledge as Power"
Instead of traditional physical upgrades, progression is tied to narrative discovery and perspective.

Reality Shifting: Gaining forbidden knowledge from the Entity changes the player's perception. This reveals hidden paths in previously explored areas (both in the temple and the village), effectively "opening" the map without needing physical keys.

Atmospheric Escalation: As players reach deeper layers of the temple, the "cozy" farming loop begins to erode. Crops mutate, weather becomes unnatural, and NPC dialogue warps, providing visual and mechanical feedback of the encroaching horror.
Narrative Asymmetry & The Entity
The heart of the game is the player's relationship with the Great Old One residing within the temple.
Cryptic Communication: The Entity does not offer traditional quests. It communicates through abstract puzzles, environmental shifts, and psychological tests that the player must interpret.

Tragic NPC Dynamics: As the player grows closer to the Entity, their perception of the village changes. Hidden cultist ties are revealed, turning a simple "dating sim" into a high-stakes psychological drama where the people you helped might be part of a cosmic cycle.
Project Overview: Gears of the Behemoth (Working Title)
Genre: Third-Person Action / Boss-Rush / Adventure
The Design Challenge: Merging the grand scale of "Titan" encounters with complex mechanical dismantling puzzles, set within a gritty, resource-driven industrial world.

Core Concept: In a world where giant mechanical "Colossi" roam the landscape as moving factories and war machines, the player must utilize specialized steampunk vehicles to chase, scale, and deactivate these behemoths from the inside out.
My Role: Concept & System Designer
Inspirations: Shadow of The Colossus
The Vehicle-to-Colossus Loop
The core gameplay defines a seamless transition between high-speed pursuit and vertical platforming.

Specialized Steampunk Vehicles: Players use customized machines (steam-bikes, grappling-tanks) that serve dual purposes: navigation in an open world and acting as mobile platforms to launch the player onto moving targets.

Momentum-Based Climbing: Navigation relies on steam-powered grappling hooks and hydraulic pistons. Players must master their "Steam Pressure" (stamina) management to scale the shifting mechanical exterior without being shaken off.
Puzzle-Based Boss Encounters
The Colossi are not just enemies to be defeated; they are complex, moving environmental puzzles.
Internal Sabotage: The primary objective is to reach critical components—such as overheating boilers, exposed gears, or central clockwork cores.

Weak Point Progression: Players must dismantle outer armor plates or redirect steam valves to expose deep-seated weak points. Success relies on observation and mechanical logic rather than brute force.
Industrial Atmosphere & Scale
Visual and narrative design is built around the overwhelming scale of the industrial era.
Mechanical Living World: Colossi function as mining harvesters or refineries. Their designs (pipes, brass, soot) and rhythmic mechanical sounds create a cohesive, immersive industrial aesthetic.

Risk vs. Reward Scavenging: Beyond deactivation, players can choose to "scavenge" rare components during the climb. This adds a layer of depth for players who want to upgrade their own gear and vehicles, at the risk of falling.
Project Overview: Mikapoly
Genre: 2-Player Cooperative Tabletop / Resource Management

Core Concept: A delicate balancing act where two players manage their individual resource pools to collaboratively reach 100 Happiness Points (Win Condition) before their shared 100 Monotony Points (Loss Condition) meter fills up and ends the game.

The Design Challenge: Transforming the traditional, elimination-based mechanics of Monopoly into a highly cooperative, positive-sum experience without losing the tension of resource scarcity and basic mechanics of movement and purchasing of the base game.
Inspration: I ceated this game as a gift that we can play and remember for my girlfriend, using our memories of 7-year relationship while still giving myself a meaningful challenge.
Note: All numbers and other values are determined by playing the game iterativly with my other designer friends.
The Dual Economy: Individual Resources vs. Shared Goals

To create meaningful cooperation, the game utilizes an asymmetric economy. Players do not share a single bank; instead, each player must manage their own distinct resource pools: Time, Effort, and Trust.
Unlocking Memory Zones: The traditional 28 properties have been replaced with "Memory Zones." As players navigate the board, they must spend their individual resources to unlock these zones.

The Cooperative Yield: Successfully unlocking a zone does not generate personal wealth. Instead, it rewards the team with shared Happiness Points. This design creates a core loop where individual sacrifice directly fuels the collective victory condition, forcing constant communication about who can afford to buy which zone.
Rent Mechanics & The Monotony Threat
The most significant design shift was reimagining Monopoly's punishing "Rent" system into a mechanic that tests resource allocation rather than creating player bankruptcy.
The Sharing Fee: When a player lands on a Memory Zone previously unlocked by their partner, they must pay a "Sharing Fee" from their individual resource pool.

The Loss Condition (Monotony): If a player is completely drained of resources and cannot afford the Sharing Fee, they are not eliminated. Instead, the failure penalizes the team by increasing the shared Monotony Meter.

Design Perspective: This mechanic is the primary source of tension. It actively punishes players for letting their partner's resources drop to zero. To survive, players must strategically plan their routes and ensure that neither player becomes completely impoverished, turning every turn into a calculated risk against the looming threat of reaching 100 Monotony Points.

Fun Interaction: Players do not get to build houses or hotels over the board, but after collecting all zone of the same set, they can either tell a story or show an old photo related to that zone to raise the rent by 2 unit of any one of the resources!
